title: Tandem vs Legacy Commercial Real Estate Brokers | Tandem
summary: Compare Tandem's AI-native leasing process to legacy brokers like CBRE and JLL. Find office space 6x faster with access to 30% more listings.
body_text: Working with a legacy commercial real estate broker — CBRE, JLL, Newmark, Cushman & Wakefield, and so on — typically takes 90 to 180 days to place a startup in a new office, and indexes highly on the listings those firms control. Tandem, an AI-native office leasing brokerage backed by Y Combinator, has placed 500+ companies in offices in an average of 27 days, with access to 30% more spaces than traditional broker networks. If you're a business owner or founder looking for private office space, that gap is worth understanding before you make any calls. --- What a Legacy Commercial Real Estate Broker Actually Does To compare Tandem vs. legacy brokers fairly, you need to understand what the incumbents are built for. Firms like CBRE, JLL, Newmark, Cushman & Wakefield, and Colliers are full-service commercial real estate firms. Their bread and butter is large enterprise tenants: law firms signing 20,000 sqft for 10 years, financial institutions negotiating entire floors in Class A towers. That's where the commission math works best. A 2,000 sqft startup lease generates a fraction of the fee a Fortune 500 deal does, which means your search often lands with a junior broker, competes for attention against bigger mandates, and moves at whatever pace a firm built for enterprise clients is willing to move. A few other structural quirks matter for founders: Listing control : Legacy brokers earn larger commissions on spaces where they also represent the landlord. That conflict shapes what they show you. Relationship silos : Each firm hires brokers as independent contractors. Each broker has their own set of relationships and people that they like to do business with. No single broker sees the whole market. No startup specialization : Most traditional brokers don't speak equity, burn rate, or Good Guy Guarantees. They're built for balance sheets and income statements, not venture funding and cap tables. None of this makes legacy brokers incompetent or unimportant. It can, however, make them misaligned with what an an early-to-mid stage startup actually needs. --- How Tandem's Approach Differs From a Traditional Office Broker Tandem is like an office brokerage on steroids. Every Tandem agent is backed by an agentic brain that knows the whole market: what's available, what asking rates are, what other deals closed for in the building, which spaces are about to come to market, and what landlords are likely to give the most. Tandem's AI lets everyone work with a best-in-class broker, regardless of the size of office you're looking for. Tandem aggregates supply across three space types — private leases, shared spaces, and subleases — and layers in AI market intelligence to surface options that match your actual requirements: headcount, budget in $/sqft/year, neighborhood preference, and lease-length flexibility. Here's what that looks like in practice: 30%+ more inventory. Tandem has built direct relationships with landlords, host companies offering shared space, and sublessors across NYC, San Francisco, and Boston. That means it surfaces options that never appear in any single traditional broker's pipeline. You're not limited to one firm's portfolio. 27-day average placement. The industry average for an office lease runs 90–180 days through a legacy firm. Tandem's process — from first tour to signed agreement — averages 27 days. That matters when you've just raised a Series A and need to stop working out of a WeWork before your new engineers show up on day one. Free to you. Like traditional brokers, Tandem is compensated by the landlord or host company. Startup-native expertise. Tandem advisors have worked with dozens of startups, including Cursor, Upwork, Volta, and countless others. For a deeper walkthrough of the leasing process, see our guide for how to rent office space as a startup . --- What Types of Office Space Can You Find Through Tandem vs. a Traditional Broker? Legacy brokers focus almost exclusively on direct leases — you signing with a landlord for a fixed term. That's the right product for some startups. But it's not the only product, and traditional firms rarely give you a clean comparison across all three options. Tandem surfaces all three space types in a single search: Space Type Typical Lease Length Who Signs With Speed to Move In Customization Private Lease 12–36+ months Tenant + Landlord 4–12 weeks High (buildout possible) Shared Space Month-to-month to 12 months Tenant + Host Company 1–3 weeks Low Sublease Fixed (remainder of original term) Tenant + Sublessor 2–6 weeks Low to medium A traditional broker will almost never show you a shared space — there's no landlord commission to collect. Tandem shows you all three because the goal is finding the right space for your team's stage and risk tolerance, not maximizing transaction size. For a seed-stage team of 8 moving into their first real office, a shared space in Flatiron or SoMa might be the right call. For a 25-person Series B team that needs its own identity, a private lease in NoMad or SoHo makes more sense. --- How AI Market Intelligence Changes the Office Search Traditional brokerage is relationship-driven and opaque. A broker knows what their colleagues have toured recently, which landlords are flexible on terms, and which buildings have ghost listings sitting vacant. That institutional knowledge is valuable — but it's tribal, slow to update, and not shared with you in any systematic way. Tandem's AI-powered leasing layer does something different: it aggregates market data across available inventory, pricing signals, neighborhood trends, and comparable lease economics to surface recommendations matched to your actual inputs — not the broker's existing relationships or commission priorities. Practically, this means: You see more options, faster, ranked by fit rather than by who the broker knows Pricing is transparent: if private offices in the Mission are running $45–$65/sqft/year, you see that before you make an offer Historical lease velocity data shows how quickly spaces in a given neighborhood move — useful when you're deciding whether to jump on a Tribeca loft or wait on a second option in Chelsea --- The Tandem Process vs. Working With CBRE, JLL, or Newmark Here's what a typical startup office search actually looks like through each path. The traditional broker process You call a firm, get assigned to a broker (often junior) Broker runs a needs assessment, shares a PDF of available listings — their listings Multiple tours scheduled over 3–6 weeks You choose a space, broker drafts an LOI Landlord counters; negotiation runs 2–6 weeks Lease drafts exchanged; attorney review (your cost) adds more time Total timeline: 90–180 days , sometimes longer The Tandem process You browse available spaces directly on Tandem or connect with a Tandem agent Tandem surfaces matched options instantaneously from the entire market's availability Curated tours scheduled quickly — typically within the first 24-72 hours Tandem handles LOI drafting and negotiation coordination on your behalf You sign directly with the landlord or host company Total timeline: average 27 days --- The Real Cost Differences Between Tandem and a Legacy Broker The commission structure looks similar on the surface — both are paid by the landlord, not by you. But the economics diverge in a few meaningful ways. Negotiation outcomes. Legacy brokers sometimes have dual representation conflicts, working both sides of the same transaction. Tandem represents you exclusively, which tends to produce better lease terms, lower deposits, and more landlord concessions. Hidden cost exposure. Founders using traditional brokers often discover mid-lease that HVAC overtime fees, after-hours access charges, or TI allowance shortfalls were never flagged upfront. Tandem's diligence process surfaces these before you sign. Opportunity cost. A 150-day search instead of a 27-day search isn't just slower — it's a distraction from building your company. For early-stage teams, that's real money. If you're thinking about getting an office soon, reach out to us at team@tandem.space to get your search started, or browse a sample of what's on the market at tandemspace.com. --- Last updated: August 2026

title: When Should Kids Get the Flu Shot? A Pediatrician's Timing Guide (2026-27)
summary: Pediatrician's timing guide for the 2026-27 kids' flu shot. Late September through October is the target window. Two-dose rule and RSV co-admin explained.
body_text: Last medically reviewed: 2026-08-08 For most kids, the sweet spot is late September through October. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a yearly flu shot for every child 6 months and older, with both doses done by October 31 if this is a first flu season (two doses, four weeks apart). If you miss October, still get it. Flu often circulates into spring . Every September in our telehealth visits, we hear the same question: "Are we early, or are we already behind?" The honest answer is reassuring for almost every family. Below, a pediatrician walks you through the exact flu vaccine timing for kids, the two-dose rule most parents don't know about, and what to do if you missed the October window. Not sure if your child needs one dose or two? Talk to a pediatrician Key Takeaways The best time for kids to get a flu shot is September or October, with vaccination done by the end of October. Children 6 months through 8 years who have never had two lifetime flu shots need two doses this year, given four weeks apart. First-time vaccinees should start in early September so both doses fit inside the window. The flu shot can be given at the same visit as the RSV antibody (nirsevimab), COVID vaccine, and routine baby shots. Kids with egg allergy can get any age-appropriate flu vaccine, no special precautions, no observation period. If you missed October, still get it. Flu often circulates into spring. Blueberry Pediatrics follows the AAP, which continues to recommend a yearly flu shot for all children 6 months and older. The Short Answer: When Should Kids Get the Flu Shot? The best time for kids to get a flu shot in 2026 is late September through the end of October. The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) says vaccination should ideally be offered in September or October, and everyone 6 months and older should be vaccinated by the end of October. Not too early, not too late. For a child who only needs one dose, July or August is not preferred, since the immune boost can wane before flu peaks in December through February. But if October comes and goes, do not skip. A November, December, or even January shot still protects. First-time vaccinees are the exception. They need two doses, four weeks apart, so dose one should be as soon as vaccine is available, usually early to mid September. Same-visit is fine. The flu vaccine can go in the same visit as the RSV antibody nirsevimab, the COVID vaccine, and routine childhood vaccines. When Is the 2026-27 Flu Vaccine Available? Most pediatricians and pharmacies begin stocking the 2026-27 flu vaccine in August, and supply is usually broad by early September. If you call your pediatrician's office in mid August and vaccine has not landed, ask when the first shipment is expected, and the office can usually give you a date. For most kids, August is possible but not preferred: a single-dose child risks the immune boost waning before flu peaks, and a first-time vaccinee is better off starting in early September. Retail pharmacies routinely give the flu shot to kids 3 and up (age minimums vary by state and chain); for babies and toddlers under 3, the pediatrician's office is almost always the right place. Does My Child Need One Dose or Two? The Two-Dose Rule Most Parents Miss This is the piece of flu-vaccine timing that catches families off guard. The rule, in plain language: Children 6 months through 8 years need two doses this season if they have not previously received at least two total lifetime doses before July 1. Everyone 9 and older gets one dose, regardless of history. Decision box: Has your child ever had at least two flu shots in their life? Yes: One dose this year. No, or not sure: Two doses this year, four weeks apart. Age 9 and up: One dose, regardless of history. The two lifetime doses do not need to be in the same season or in back-to-back years. What matters is that a child has been "primed" with two doses of any flu vaccine at some point, at least four weeks apart, before July 1 of this year. Edge case: a child who is 8 at their first dose and turns 9 before dose two is due should still get both doses, because the rule is based on age at dose one. The Scheduling Math for First-Time Vaccinees If your child needs two doses this year, the timing works out like this: Dose two must be given at least 28 days after dose one. To have both done by October 31, dose one needs to be no later than the last week of September. That is why our pediatricians tell first-time families to book dose one in early to mid September, which gives comfortable margin. For a baby turning 6 months mid-season (November or December), you do not wait for next year. Dose one at the 6-month visit, dose two four weeks later, and they are protected for the second half of the season. When Can a Baby Get the Flu Shot? The earliest age is 6 months. Every child 6 months and older without a medical contraindication should get an annual flu vaccine. That is the standing recommendation from the American Academy of Pediatrics and the federal ACIP. Below 6 months, babies cannot receive the flu vaccine. Two layers of protection matter: Vaccination in pregnancy. A pregnant person can safely get the flu shot in any trimester; antibodies cross the placenta and protect the baby for the first few months of life. Cocooning. Vaccinating everyone in the household, plus regular caregivers and grandparents, reduces the odds that flu reaches the baby. The AAP HealthyChildren page on protecting babies from flu walks through the same playbook. A note that trips up new parents: the RSV antibody (nirsevimab, brand name Beyfortus) protects against RSV, not flu. For flu, the shot at 6 months is your baby's first real defense. Can My Child Get the Flu Shot With Other Vaccines? Yes. This is one of the most common September telehealth questions. The flu vaccine can be given at the same visit as the RSV antibody (nirsevimab), the COVID vaccine, and routine childhood immunizations. Injectable vaccines go in separate anatomic sites, at least an inch apart. Nirsevimab is a monoclonal antibody, not a vaccine. It goes in a separate syringe at a separate site; it cannot be mixed with the flu vaccine, but it does not need to be spaced apart. Safety and side effects match giving each alone. For babies under 8 months at the start of RSV season, the fall visit is often where both protections happen: one trip, one appointment, two layers of defense. Shot vs. Nasal Spray: Which Is Better for Kids? Both are acceptable, and neither is preferred over the other when both are age-appropriate. Pick what your pediatrician has in stock and what your child tolerates best. Age matters for the nasal spray. FluMist, the live-attenuated nasal spray, is only approved for ages 2 through 49. Under 2, the shot is the only option. Not everyone can get the nasal spray. It is not for pregnant people, kids with certain immune conditions, and a few other groups spelled out in the ACIP guidance. Your pediatrician will tell you if the spray is not an option for your child. Same strains in both. The shot and the spray protect against the same 2026-27 strains this year. What About Egg Allergy? Egg allergy is a much smaller deal than parents expect, and a lot of families are still working from older, stricter advice. Any child with an egg allergy, mild or severe, can receive any age-appropriate flu vaccine (egg-based or egg-free) with no special precautions beyond those for any vaccine: no egg-free clinic, no observation period, no allergist visit required just because of egg. This matches current AAP guidance on which flu vaccine children should get . Egg allergy is not the same as a prior flu-vaccine reaction If your child has ever had a severe allergic reaction to a flu vaccine itself (not to egg), that is different. Talk to your pediatrician or an allergist before this year's shot. A history of anaphylaxis to a previous flu vaccine is a contraindication. Keep those two things separate: egg allergy, get the shot. Prior severe reaction to a flu vaccine, call your pediatrician first. What's New in the 2026-27 Flu Vaccine? All three strains in this year's vaccine were updated. On March 13, 2026, the FDA recommended changing all three components to better match a fast-drifting strain called H3N2 subclade K, which spread widely during the 2025-26 season. The details are in the CDC's ACIP flu vaccine summary of recommendations . New strains, same schedule. Dosing, timing, age, and safety guidance for this year are the same as last year. Only the composition changed. All U.S. flu vaccines are trivalent this season. They cover two influenza A strains plus one influenza B strain. The second B strain (B/Yamagata) that was in older four-component (quadrivalent) vaccines was dropped a few years ago and remains dropped. Supply is expected to be adequate. The FDA anticipates a sufficient and diverse supply for 2026-27. A note on the 2026 federal vaccine schedule. You may have seen news this year about changes to the federal childhood immunization schedule. Blueberry Pediatrics follows the American Academy of Pediatrics, which continues to recommend a yearly flu shot for all children 6 months and older. If your pediatrician recommends the flu shot for your child this fall, that recommendation is based on the AAP's 2026 schedule. If you have questions about how the news affects your child, ask us. How Well Does It Work? In a typical season, the flu vaccine reduces a child's risk of getting sick from flu by roughly 40 to 60 percent, and it is even better at preventing severe illness and hospitalization. The CDC's mid-season interim estimate for children in the 2025-26 season showed the vaccine cut outpatient visits by 38 to 41 percent and reduced hospitalization by 41 percent. Season-specific numbers for 2026-27 will not exist until well into the season. Even in a lower-effectiveness year, the vaccine still does the most important job: keeping kids out of the hospital. What if We Missed the End of October? Is It Too Late? No. This is one of the most common late-fall questions our telehealth pediatricians get, and the honest answer is reassuring. Flu commonly circulates through winter and into spring, with peaks anywhere from December through March. A shot given in November, December, or even January still protects during the months you need it most. The reason to aim for October is to have full protection built up before flu really starts moving, not because the vaccine "expires" after that date. If you missed October, do this now. It takes about two weeks after the shot for full protection to kick in, and every week you wait is a week of exposure with no coverage. When to Call Your Pediatrician Reach out to your pediatrician (or start a telehealth visit) if any of these apply: Your baby is turning 6 months this fall and you want to plan the two-dose series. Your child had a reaction to a flu vaccine in a previous year (not the same as an egg allergy). Your child has a chronic condition (asthma, heart or lung disease, immune conditions, neurologic conditions) and you want to talk through timing. You are pregnant and want to talk through timing of your own flu shot. You missed October and are not sure whether to still get one. You are not sure if this counts as your child's first flu season, or how many lifetime doses they have had. Your child is coming down with something this fall and you want to tell the difference between a cold and the flu before deciding what to do next. Timing questions before your child's flu shot? Start a visit How to Book a Flu Shot for Your Child You have three places to book: Your pediatrician's office. Best for babies, toddlers, and any child with a chronic condition, because your child's full history is on file, and the office can slot the flu shot into a scheduled well visit. A retail pharmacy. For older kids and teens (typical minimum is age 3; varies by state and chain), pharmacies are convenient and often have same-week openings. Check with your pediatrician first if your child has a complex history. Blueberry Pediatrics. If you're a Blueberry family, message us. We can pull up your child's history, confirm whether this is a one-dose or two-dose year, and help you plan the fall visit. Flu-shot timing sounds simple until you sit down with a 5-month-old who will be 6 months in November, or a first-grader who has had exactly one flu shot in their life. You do not have to figure it out on your own. FAQ When should kids get the flu shot in 2026? Late September through October 31 for most children. First-time vaccinees (6 months through 8 years) should start in early September so both doses fit inside the window. Does my child need one or two flu shots this year? Children 6 months through 8 years need two doses if they have never had at least two total lifetime flu shots before July 1. Everyone 9 and up gets one dose. Not sure of your child's history? Call your pediatrician. How far apart do the two flu shots need to be? At least 4 weeks (28 days). Can my child get the flu shot and the RSV shot at the same visit? Yes. Nirsevimab is a separate syringe at a separate site, but it can be given at the same visit as the flu shot and any routine baby shots. Can kids with egg allergy get the flu shot? Yes, without special precautions. A previous severe reaction to a flu vaccine itself is a different question and needs a pediatrician or allergist call first. Is the nasal spray as good as the flu shot? For kids 2 and older who can get it, yes. Neither is preferred. Under age 2, only the shot is an option. What if we missed October? Still get it. A November, December, or January shot still protects. Do not wait for next year. How early can kids get the flu shot in August? Vaccine is often available in August, but we recommend waiting for September so the immune boost does not wane before flu peaks. For first-timers who need two doses, early September is the earliest we usually recommend. Should I be worried about news about the CDC flu schedule this year? Blueberry Pediatrics follows the American Academy of Pediatrics, which continues to recommend a yearly flu shot for all children 6 months and older. If you have specific questions, ask your pediatrician. Where can I get my child's flu shot? Your pediatrician's office is easiest for babies and toddlers. Pharmacies cover older kids and teens. title: Qnity Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results, Raises Full-Year Financial Guidance
summary: – Second quarter net sales of $1.4 billion, up 22% year-over-year, organic sales(1) up 22% – GAAP net income of $136 million, down…...
body_text: Qnity Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results, Raises Full-Year Financial Guidance August 04, 2026 6:00am EDT Download as PDF Related Documents Earnings Webcast Audio Presentation PDF – Second quarter net sales of $1.4 billion, up 22% year-over-year, organic sales(1) up 22% – GAAP net income of $136 million, down 31% year-over-year; Adjusted Earnings(1) of $250 million, up 53% year-over-year – Adjusted Operating EBITDA(1) of $431 million, up 24% year-over-year – GAAP EPS of $0.59, down 34% year-over-year; Adjusted EPS(1) of $1.19, up 53% year-over-year – Raises full year 2026 financial guidance WILMINGTON, Del.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Qnity Electronics, Inc. (“Qnity”) (NYSE: Q) today reported results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “We delivered our ninth consecutive quarter of profitable growth driven by disciplined execution across both segments,” said Jon Kemp, Qnity’s Chief Executive Officer. “The continued momentum reflects our deep alignment with the industry’s most advanced technology roadmaps, our embedded role in customers’ next-generation platforms, and our ability to deliver the solutions they need at scale.” Kemp added, “The industry shift toward shrink and stack is lengthening the journey every chip takes, requiring more process complexity and more layers, creating a multiplier effect for materials intensity. Qnity sits at the center of this trend with one of the broadest portfolios of end-to-end solutions across the stack. As AI, high-performance computing and advanced connectivity reshape demand, we are uniquely positioned to continue enhancing value for customers and deliver long-term growth for our shareholders.” Financial Results Summary In millions, except per share amounts GAAP Results Q2 2026 (1) Q2 2025 (2) Net Sales $ 1,429 $ 1,170 Semiconductor Technologies 744 644 Interconnect Solutions 685 526 Gross Profit $ 666 $ 540 Net Income $ 136 $ 198 Diluted Earnings Per Share $ 0.59 $ 0.90 Non-GAAP Results Adjusted Gross Profit $ 666 $ 542 Adjusted Operating EBITDA $ 431 $ 347 Adjusted Earnings, net of tax $ 250 $ 163 Adjusted Earnings Per Share $ 1.19 $ 0.78 (1) Organic Sales, Adjusted Gross Profit, Adjusted Operating EBITDA, Adjusted Earnings, and Adjusted EPS are non-GAAP measures. See “Non-GAAP Measures” for further discussion, including a definition of significant items. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measure, including details of significant items, can be found in the “Non-GAAP Measures” section of this press release. (2) Q2 2025 is presented on a pro forma basis. The Pro Forma non-GAAP measures give effect to pro forma adjustments related to interest expense associated with our current indebtedness, agreements executed in connection with the spin-off from DuPont de Nemours, Inc. (“DuPont”) and other standalone costs as if the spin-off had occurred on January 1, 2025. See “Non-GAAP Measures” for further discussion, including a definition of significant items. Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measure, including details of significant items, can be found in the “Non-GAAP Measures” section of this press release. Refer to the “Non-GAAP Measures” section of this press release for further details on these adjustments. Guidance for Full Year 2026 Qnity is raising full‑year guidance based on strong second‑quarter performance and continued near‑term momentum, including strong customer engagement and demand across end markets. Qnity’s full year 2026 guidance (3) is as follows: Net Sales $5.55B - $5.65B Adjusted Operating EBITDA $1.675B - $1.725B Adjusted EPS $4.40 - $4.60 Adjusted Free Cash Flow $600M - $700M (3) We calculate forward-looking Adjusted Operating EBITDA, Adjusted EPS, and Adjusted Free Cash Flow based on internal forecasts that exclude certain information that would be included in the most directly comparable forward-looking GAAP measures. We are not providing a quantitative reconciliation of forward-looking Non-GAAP financial measures to the corresponding GAAP financial measure for these measures due to the unreasonable effort and uncertainty in estimating certain items necessary for such reconciliations, including adjustments that could be made for significant items, interest expense, indirect legacy costs/benefits, transformation, integration, and other charges, share-based compensation amounts, non-recurring, unusual or unanticipated charges, expenses or gains. Conference Call and Webcast Information Qnity will hold a conference call to review these results on Tuesday, August 4, 2026, at 8:00 a.m. ET. Investors can join the conference call via telephone by dialing (800) 343-5172 (domestic) or +1 (203) 518-9856 (international) and using the participant code QNITY. An audio-only live webcast, presentation materials, and replay will also be made available at Events | Qnity Electronics, Inc. (Q) . About Qnity Qnity is a premier technology provider across the semiconductor value chain, empowering AI, high performance computing, and advanced connectivity. From groundbreaking solutions for semiconductor chip manufacturing, to enabling high-speed transmission within complex electronic systems, our high-performance materials and integration expertise make tomorrow’s technologies possible. More information about the company, its businesses and solutions can be found at http://www.qnityelectronics.com . Qnity™, the Qnity Node Logo, and all products, unless otherwise noted, denoted with TM or ® are trademarks, trade names or registered trademarks of affiliates of Qnity Electronics, Inc. Forward-looking statements use words such as "plans", "expects", "will", "would", "anticipates", "believes", "intends", "seeks", "projects", "efforts", "estimates", "potential", "continue", "intend", “outlook”, "may", "could", "should" and similar expressions, among others, as well as other words or expressions referencing future events, conditions or circumstances. Additional information concerning risks and uncertainties can be found in Qnity's filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”), including under the headings “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” and “Risk Factors” in our most recent Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) on February 26, 2026, and in Qnity’s future filings with the SEC. Any forward-looking statement speaks only as of the date on which it is made. Qnity does not undertake any obligation to publicly update or revise any forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise, except as required by applicable law. Non-GAAP Financial Measures This press release includes information that does not conform to accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”) and are considered non-GAAP measures, including the presentation of Organic Sales, Adjusted Gross Profit, Adjusted Pro Forma Gross Profit, Adjusted Operating EBITDA, Adjusted Pro Forma Operating EBITDA, Adjusted Operating EBITDA Margin, Adjusted Pro Forma Operating EBITDA Margin, Adjusted Earnings, Adjusted Pro Forma Earnings, Adjusted EPS, Adjusted Pro Forma EPS, Base Tax Rate, Adjusted Free Cash Flow, Adjusted Pro Forma Free Cash Flow, Adjusted Pro Forma Base Tax Rate. The non-GAAP measures presented are not necessarily indicative of the future possible key performance indicators or non-GAAP measures of Qnity. Qnity believes these non-GAAP financial measures are useful to investors because they provide additional information related to the performance of Qnity on an as-managed basis by DuPont and a stand-alone basis. These non-GAAP financial measures supplement disclosures prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP and reflect results in a manner that enables, in some instances, more meaningful analysis of trends and facilitates comparison of results across periods. These non-GAAP financial measures should not be viewed as an alternative to U.S. GAAP. Furthermore, such non-GAAP measures may not be consistent with similar measures provided or used by other companies. Reconciliations for these non-GAAP measures to their most directly comparable U.S. GAAP financial measures are provided below. Non-GAAP measures included in this press release are defined below. Adjusted Earnings is defined as net income available for Qnity common stockholders excluding the impacts of significant items, amortization expense of intangibles, non-operating pension / other post-employment benefits (“OPEB”) credits / costs, and indirect legacy costs / benefits and adjusted for the income tax effect of these excluded items. Adjusted Earnings is the numerator used in the calculation of Adjusted EPS. Adjusted EPS is defined as Adjusted Earnings per common share - diluted. Base Tax Rate is a non-GAAP measure defined as the GAAP Effective Tax Rate excluding the tax rate impacts of adjustments to net income available for Qnity common stockholders in determining Adjusted Earnings. Adjusted Operating EBITDA is defined as Pre-tax Earnings (i.e., “Income before income taxes") before interest, depreciation, amortization, non-operating pension / OPEB benefits credits / costs, foreign exchange gains / losses, indirect legacy costs / benefits, and adjusted for significant items. Adjusted Operating EBITDA Margin is defined as Adjusted Operating EBITDA divided by Net Sales. Adjusted Free Cash Flow is defined as cash provided by/used for operating activities less capital expenditures and excluding the impact of indirect legacy costs / benefits related to cost sharing arrangements executed between DuPont and Qnity at the time of spin-off, IT independence costs, and transformation, integration, and other charges, as well as cash inflows/outflows that are unusual in nature and/or infrequent in occurrence that neither relate to the ordinary course of the Company's underlying business liquidity. Significant items are items that impact Qnity and arise outside the ordinary course of business that management believes may cause misinterpretation of underlying business performance, both historical and future, based on a combination of some or all of the item’s size, unusual nature and infrequent occurrence. Within this definition, Management classifies as significant items certain costs and expenses associated with transformation, integration, and other charges related to transformational activities, including acquisitions and divestitures, as they are considered unrelated to ongoing business performance. Indirect legacy costs/benefits relate to cost sharing arrangements executed between DuPont and Qnity at the time of the spin-off. Such costs include certain litigation and environmental-related shared costs, taxes, and indirect cost sharing arrangements, and are excluded from Adjusted Earnings, Adjusted Operating EBITDA, and Adjusted Free Cash Flow, as defined above, as they are considered unrelated to ongoing Qnity business performance. Organic Sales is defined as net sales excluding the impacts of currency and portfolio actions. Adjusted gross profit is calculated as Gross Profit (net sales less cost of sales), excluding the impact of Significant items on Net Sales and Cost of Sales and the impact on Cost of Sales from certain services associated with transaction agreements entered with DuPont, including the Transition Services Agreement, certain product service agreements, contract manufacturing agreements, raw materials supply agreements, and site services agreements. Qnity has also presented measures on a pro forma basis which were prepared in a manner consistent with Article 11 of Regulation S-X. Our pro forma results give effect to the spin-off and related transactions as if the Spin Off occurred on January 1, 2025. Our Pro Forma adjustments reflect: Interest expense associated with our current debt structure; Income tax effect of incremental interest expense; The impact of the Transition Services Agreements and other commercial agreements entered into with DuPont in connection with the spin-off; and Transaction and other incremental costs required to operate as a stand-alone entity. We believe pro forma measures are helpful to supplement our financial results as they allow a comparison of results as a stand-alone company as if the agreements were in place for the periods presented. Adjusted Pro Forma Earnings is defined as net income available for Qnity common stockholders excluding the impacts of significant items, amortization expense of intangibles, non-operating pension / other post-employment benefits credits / costs, and indirect legacy costs / benefits, less the after-tax impacts of the pro forma adjustments described above and adjusted for the income tax effect of these excluded items. Adjusted Pro Forma Earnings is the numerator used in the calculation of Adjusted Pro Forma EPS. Adjusted Pro Forma EPS is defined as Adjusted Pro Forma Earnings per common share - diluted. Adjusted Pro Forma Base Tax Rate is a non‑GAAP measure defined as the Base Tax Rate adjusted to reflect the estimated income tax effects of the pro forma adjustments described above. Adjusted Pro Forma Operating EBITDA is defined as Adjusted Operating EBITDA less certain pro forma adjustments described above. Adjusted Pro Forma Operating EBITDA Margin is defined as Adjusted Pro Forma Operating EBITDA divided by Net Sales. Adjusted Pro Forma Free Cash Flow is defined as pro forma cash provided by/used for operating activities less capital expenditures and excluding the impact of indirect legacy costs / benefits related to cost sharing arrangements executed between DuPont and Qnity at the time of spin-off, IT independence costs, transformation, integration, and other charges, and transaction and other incremental costs required to operate as a stand-alone entity, as well as cash inflows/outflows that are unusual in nature and/or infrequent in occurrence that neither relate to the ordinary course of the Company's underlying business liquidity. Adjusted Pro Forma Gross Profit is calculated as Gross Profit (net sales less cost of sales), excluding the impact on Cost of Sales from certain services associated with transaction agreements entered with DuPont, including the Transition Services Agreement, certain product service agreements, contract manufacturing agreements, raw materials supply agreements, and site services agreements. title: Cintas Earns Place on U.S. News & World Report’s List of 2026-2027 Best Companies to Work For
summary: CINCINNATI, Ohio – Cintas Corporation (Nasdaq: CTAS) has been recognized by U.S. News & World Report as one of the nation’s 2026-2027 Best Companies to Work For.
body_text: CINCINNATI, Ohio – Cintas Corporation (Nasdaq: CTAS) has been recognized by U.S. News & World Report as one of the nation’s 2026-2027 Best Companies to Work For . "This award is a meaningful honor because it reflects the experience of our employee-partners," said Todd Schneider, President and CEO of Cintas. "Cintas’ culture has always set us apart, and this recognition reflects our continued focus on creating opportunities for growth, development and success. The dedication of our employee-partners is the driving force behind our performance, and we remain committed to making Cintas a place where great people can build rewarding careers." The rating recognizes the top 25% of companies after an evaluation of 3,900 publicly and privately owned organizations across the following categories: Quality of pay and benefits Work-life balance and flexibility Job and company stability Physical and psychological comfort Belongingness and esteem Career opportunities and professional development. Cintas earned the highest possible score in the stability category. About Cintas Corporation Cintas Corporation helps more than one million businesses of all types and sizes get Ready™ to open their doors with confidence every day by providing workwear and business essentials that help keep their customers’ facilities and employees clean, safe, and looking their best. With offerings including workwear and business essentials such as uniforms, mats, mops, towels, restroom supplies, workplace water services, first aid and safety products, eye-wash stations, safety training, fire extinguishers, sprinkler systems and alarm service, Cintas helps customers get Ready for the Workday® . Headquartered in Cincinnati, Cintas is a publicly held Fortune 500 company traded over the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol CTAS and is a component of both the Standard & Poor’s 500 Index and Nasdaq-100 Index.

title: The $4 Million Fast Pass Through the Panama Canal
summary: Discover Flexport APIs and EDIs to speed, scale, and optimize your supply chain. Developer tools make it easy to instantly access logistics data and vital cargo and global trade documentation in the Flexport Platform or your ERP.
body_text: Somebody paid $4 million on Monday for the right to move a ship through the Panama Canal ahead of everyone else. The buyer was the owner of the Seaspan Benefactor, a 10,010 TEU container ship, that’s $800 per container (FEU). What that money bought was one auctioned transit slot, at a price that came in near a record and well above anything the previous week had produced. For context, vessels are currently sitting roughly 10 days before they get a crossing. That's the worst backlog on the Pacific-to-Atlantic run since May. Check out Flexport Atlas for live monitoring. We appreciate the dedication to on-time performance Flexport has 30 containers aboard the Seaspan Benefactor across 14 clients. ONE (Ocean Network Express) operates the ship on the Premier Alliance and Evergreen loop from Asia to the US East Coast. The ship’s recent track runs through South Korea before the leg toward Panama, and has been holding at anchor in the Gulf of Panama waiting to head north. We've always appreciated ONE's dedication to on-time performance. Turns out that dedication has a going rate, and this week the going rate was seven figures. Respect. Anyone who's stood in a theme park queue at 2pm in July knows this trade already. One line is free and stationary. The other costs money and moves. Panama sells the same two products. The gap is that a Lightning Lane runs about thirty bucks and ends at a roller coaster, while this one ran $4 million and ends at a set of locks. What jammed up the Canal Start with the war. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz thinned out, and Bab el-Mandeb followed. All that redirected tonnage lands in the same queue as everything else. Energy and chemical cargo that used to cross the Gulf is hunting for a westbound path now, and Panama is the obvious candidate. Repairs are the second problem. Work at the locks runs into September, and part of it touches the chambers built for the biggest ships. Fewer daily transits, more ships wanting one. Rain is the third. El Niño hasn't filled the watershed the way the canal needs, so draft limits in those same chambers came down. Shallower draft means each ship carries less, and less per ship means more ships for the same volume of goods. The queue math Tuesday afternoon: 103 vessels waiting. Seventy-two of them hold a booking. The other 31 are hoping something opens up. Someone has been out there 33 days. A Super-size chemical tanker, northbound, more than a month into the wait. Then there's the part that changes how you read the $4 million. Panama's auction calendar for the balance of August shows zero slots. Nothing to bid on for the rest of the month. September 7 is the next date with anything on it, and that anything is one regular slot. Seaspan wasn't overpaying for convenience. They bought one of the last seats before the room closed for three weeks. Why a container ship? Auction slots usually go to tankers. A cargo of liquefied natural gas or refined product carries enough value that a seven-figure bid pencils out against a single voyage. Container ships work differently, which is what makes this one interesting. The Benefactor holds a position in a fixed rotation. Berth windows on the far side, feeder connections, chassis and rail appointments inland, all of it scheduled around the ship showing up when it is supposed to. A missed transit doesn't cost 10 days one time. It rolls into the next sailing and the one after that, and every container that was supposed to connect misses too. Set $4 million against a whole loop of broken schedules and thousands of late containers, and the bid starts to look like math instead of desperation. What next? Expect Canal costs in your rates if you move anything through Panama, either direction. Widen your Q4 transit buffers past whatever you used last year given the current wait times. Run the West Coast discharge and intermodal comparison again. It won't win for every lane or every SKU, but enough has changed this month that a springtime answer isn't good enough anymore. Our 14 clients with freight on the Benefactor know exactly where their cargo sits. If Panama touches your network, ask us to run your options against your actual freight before the next booking window shuts.

title: Vacation Rental Guest Screening Checklist: Complete Guide 2026
summary: Vacation rental guest screening gaps cost property managers the most. Use this 2026 checklist to stop bad guests before they reach your door.
body_text: Vacation Rental Guest Screening Checklist: Complete Guide 2026 Your OTA's "Verified" badge checks identity, not intent. Here is what actually separates hosts who stop bad guests from hosts who file damage claims after the fact. Vacation rental guest screening is the process of verifying a guest's identity and evaluating their risk level before confirming a booking or handing over property access. Most vacation rental property managers and operations leads think that tightening their screening checklist or hiring a more diligent VA will solve inconsistency, because the problem is criteria or effort, not structure. Far fewer execute the second, and that gap is where the costliest incidents happen. See our AI for hospitality for how this works in practice. According to industry research, guest-caused financial loss has become routine across the sector, reflecting how widespread the problem is in 2025. Vacation rental guest screening is a two-part process: confirming that a guest is who they claim to be, then assessing whether they represent an acceptable risk to the property. Identity verification answers the first question. Risk evaluation, which examines booking patterns, profile completeness, communication tone, and payment behavior, answers the second. One without the other leaves the door open to guests who are real people with bad intentions, the profile behind most serious incidents. Screening exists to prevent four specific threats: unauthorized parties , property damage, payment fraud, and chargebacks. A guest who passes a standard name-and-photo check can still book under the pretense of a quiet family stay and host a 40-person event by midnight. Chargeback fraud, where a guest disputes a legitimate charge after checkout, is a separate exposure that identity confirmation alone does nothing to prevent. The real exposure for multi-property operators is structural, not criteria-based. A hospitality AI platform built for portfolio-scale operations recognizes what individual hosts often miss: screening quality degrades under volume. When booking requests arrive overnight or across a dozen simultaneous listings, the vetting that happens at 2pm on a Tuesday rarely matches what happens at 1am on a Friday. That inconsistency, not weak criteria, is where bad guests get through. $4.8 billion Vacation rental damage protection market, 2025 Key takeaways OTA 'Verified' badges confirm identity, not risk, the gap between what Airbnb checks and what actually protects your property is where financial exposure lives. Manual screening earns its place because automated ID verification says nothing about what a guest plans to do with your property. The first message a guest sends reveals more about intent than any ID check, how they write, what they ask, and what they omit are all signals. Less than 1% of vacation rental bookings result in a damage claim, which doesn't mean screening is working, it means screening failures are concentrated in the cases that do slip through. At volume, the failure point in any screening process is rarely the criteria, it's the gap between a booking arriving and a human actually seeing it at 1am on a Saturday across four channels. Screening removes bad actors; it does nothing for the friction good guests still experience, and most negative reviews trace back to communication failures, not property condition. Conduit closes that gap by running AI-powered guest communication continuously, from booking confirmation through checkout, so the process that screening starts doesn't collapse the moment a human isn't watching. Why OTA Platform Screening Tools (Airbnb, Vrbo, Booking.com) Aren't Enough The "Verified" badge on a guest's Airbnb profile feels reassuring. The problem is that what got checked is far narrower than most hosts assume, and the gap between what platforms verify and what actually protects your property is where real financial exposure lives. According to Airbnb's own help documentation , the platform collects email addresses, phone numbers, and government-issued ID uploads, then uses automated checks to confirm the name, photo, and document match. That is the full scope. Criminal history, sex offender registry status, prior eviction records, and damage incident databases sit entirely outside what any major OTA checks as standard. A guest can hold a verified badge and a prior property damage incident on their record simultaneously, and the platform will never surface that conflict to you. Vrbo's verification posture is materially similar. Booking.com goes further in the other direction: many rate plans require no ID verification at all, leaving hosts with even less signal before a stranger arrives. This is the limitation hosts on Booking.com, MakeMyTrip, and Goibibo encounter repeatedly: the built-in screening tools feel authoritative but deliver surprisingly little actionable risk data. "How do I effectively screen guest quality across OTA platforms like Airbnb, MakeMyTrip, Goibibo, and Booking.com? The built-in screening tools on these platforms feel insufficient or unclear to me." At a glance The badge creates confidence the underlying check doesn't warrant. The platforms are not hiding this limitation; they are built around a different incentive entirely. Airbnb's revenue depends on completed bookings. Every additional friction point in the guest flow, including a rigorous background check, risks killing a conversion. As Airbnb's own documentation frames it, verification tools are designed to build guest trust and reduce booking friction, not to hand hosts granular risk data. Airbnb's help resources on guest standards confirm that platform policies prioritize community trust at scale, a mandate that is structurally different from protecting an individual host's asset. The host's protection interest and the platform's conversion interest are structurally misaligned. Expecting one to serve the other is the core mistake. Where this misalignment hits hardest in practice is in the gap between inquiry and insight. Booking inquiries arrive overnight, after hours, and across multiple platforms simultaneously, precisely the moments when a host is least able to manually evaluate a guest's communication patterns, flag inconsistencies, or ask follow-up questions. By the time a host reviews an inquiry the next morning, the window for meaningful pre-booking screening has often already compressed. Conduit's AI Agents address this directly: they capture every booking inquiry, including those that land overnight or after hours, and deliver a first automated guest reply within days of connecting your existing SOPs and manuals, so the conversation begins immediately and the host retains a record of every exchange before a booking is confirmed. Direct booking compounds this further. A guest who books directly through your website receives zero automated identity verification unless you have independently integrated a third-party tool, a blind spot that expands proportionally as your direct booking share grows. For multi-property operators distributing across channels, these inconsistent screening postures create compounding exposure. Operating across Vrbo, Booking.com, and direct channels simultaneously means each channel's gaps stack. ai's unified Inbox consolidates all of those conversations, monitored continuously by your operations team, so no inquiry falls through the cracks of a fragmented channel stack. And because the AI Agents integrate directly with tools like Notion, Google Drive, and Airbnb, your existing documentation feeds the agent without manual re-entry, meaning the screening and communication logic you've already built into your SOPs is applied consistently across every channel, every booking, every hour. The host's protection interest and the platform's conversion interest are structurally misaligned. Manual Guest Screening Methods Every Host Should Use Before Choosing Software Automated ID verification tells you who a guest claims to be. It says nothing about what they plan to do with your property. That gap is where manual screening earns its place, and where operators who skip it pay the price in damage claims, bad reviews, and platform disputes. How the First Message Reveals More Than Any ID Check Inquiry tone is the first behavioral signal most hosts never formally evaluate. A guest who introduces themselves, names their travel purpose , and asks a specific question about the property is showing you something an algorithm cannot score: intentionality. A message that reads "is this available fri-sun" for a six-bedroom property on a holiday weekend shows you something too. Experienced hosts consistently flag vague inquiries and high-pressure requests to confirm immediately as warning signs worth a follow-up before any approval. The combination of signals matters more than any single flag. A 60-night booking request from a profile with no review history that also offers a private phone number to "sort details faster" is not three separate concerns; it is one compounding risk picture that only a human reading the full inquiry can assemble. Where volume makes this harder is exactly where the structural risk compounds. Operators managing guest communications across multiple platforms or properties simultaneously face a practical ceiling: the more inboxes you monitor, the more likely a nuanced first message slips past without the scrutiny it warrants. Conduit's Inbox centralizes those conversations so the operations or support team can monitor, review, and manage all guest communications in one place, continuously, before, during, or after a stay, rather than context-switching across platforms while behavioral signals quietly accumulate. What a Guest's Review History (or Absence of One) Actually Tells You If the message is detailed, the profile is complete, and the guest answers a follow-up question clearly, the absence of prior reviews becomes a manageable unknown rather than a hard stop. What warrants sharper scrutiny is the combination of no reviews, an incomplete profile (missing photo, unverified phone, no bio), and a vague first message. From what experienced operators consistently observe, incomplete guest profiles are linked to a disproportionate share of vacation rental damage claims, which is why they treat profile gaps as a prompt for follow-up rather than a reason to reflexively decline. The follow-up message itself, the one you send to surface more context, is where a well-configured AI Agent earns its keep. Conduit can deploy a first automated guest reply within days of connecting those materials. That means a zero-review inquiry gets a prompt, consistent, on-brand response that asks the right clarifying questions immediately, rather than sitting unanswered while a host juggles three other properties. Why Manual Screening Is a Compounding Fragility, Not a Scalable System This is the synthesis point most operator guides omit entirely: manual screening is not merely difficult to scale, it is structurally guaranteed to produce inconsistent outcomes as portfolio volume grows. Evaluating inquiry tone, zero-review profiles, and off-platform contact attempts simultaneously requires contextual interpretation that no checklist can encode, meaning the combinatorial variety of behavioral red flag combinations expands faster than any screener's capacity to apply uniform judgment across them. Diligence and experience slow the deterioration; they do not stop it. The operational model that reduces this fragility is one where guests, cleaners, contractors, and owners stay coordinated without a human sitting in every thread. Conduit's Workflows fire after trigger events in the guest lifecycle, after a booking is confirmed, after check-in, or when a specific keyword is detected, so that recurring, predictable touchpoints happen without manual staff action. This does not replace human judgment on high-signal inquiries; it reserves human judgment for them by clearing the routine volume out of the way. The Two Strategic Questions That Surface Intent Without Violating Fair Housing Rules Hosts can ask questions about the stay without asking questions about the person. Two questions do the most work: "What brings you to the area?" and "How many guests will be staying?" The first surfaces intent without touching protected characteristics. The second confirms whether the booking matches the property's registered occupancy, a house-rule enforcement question, not a demographic one. Conduit's AI Agents handle scripted follow-up questions and house-rule acknowledgments without manual re-entry, drawing from the same documentation the team already maintains. The integration keeps the screening layer consistent across properties and platforms, which is precisely where manual processes tend to drift as portfolios grow. Why Enforceable House Rules Are a Screening Instrument, Not Just a Legal Formality House rules that guests must explicitly agree to before booking function as a pre-screening layer. A minimum booking age of 25, a registered-guest-only occupancy policy, and a no-events clause all do double duty: they set legal expectations and they filter for guests who read and engage with conditions before booking. A guest who breezes past every rule on a six-bedroom holiday weekend booking is telling you something worth noting before you confirm. Red Flags to Watch for When Screening Vacation Rental Guests The signals worth acting on fall into two categories: those visible before a guest ever sends a message, and those that emerge from the conversation itself. Less than 1% of vacation rental bookings result in a damage claim, a rate that does not indicate that screening is working, but rather that screening failures are largely invisible because they manifest not as catastrophic damage events but as compounding operational costs: slower response times, missed upsells, disputed reviews, and retaliatory platform reports that erode NOI and owner relationships without triggering a formal claim. This means the real cost of poor screening is systematically undercounted, and operators who rely on claim rates as a proxy for screening effectiveness are measuring the wrong outcome entirely. The most important red flags in vacation rental guest screening are not individual alarms. They are data points in a risk score. A single flag warrants a follow-up message. Two or more flags in combination, especially when they cross identity, payment, and communication, warrant a documented decline. Where the cost of slow detection compounds fastest is in the inbox. Operators managing guest communications across multiple platforms or properties simultaneously face a version of this problem every day: a suspicious booking arrives on a Saturday night, no one is watching the channel it came in on, and an automated confirmation goes out before anyone reviews it. Conduit's Inbox is designed precisely for this scenario, centralizing conversations across platforms so that manual review, when it matters most, is not delayed by fragmented tooling. 1. Underreporting the Number of Guests at Booking One of the most common red flags in vacation rental guest screening is a guest who books for one or two people but arrives with a significantly larger group. This creates liability gaps, voids insurance coverage, and causes excessive wear on the property. Hosts should cross-reference guest count with vehicle arrivals and security camera footage. The tradeoff: some guests genuinely misunderstand per-person fee structures, so a firm but polite clarification message is essential before escalating. 2. A Completely Blank or Newly Created Guest Profile A brand-new account with zero reviews, no profile photo, and no personal bio is a meaningful screening signal during vacation rental guest screening. While many first-time guests are entirely legitimate, the combination of a blank profile with vague messaging or a local address dramatically raises risk. Hosts should ask targeted pre-booking questions to gauge intent. The tradeoff: rejecting all zero-review guests eliminates a large portion of the booking pool, so context matters enormously. 3. Requests to Move Payment Off-Platform When a guest, or someone posing as a host, pushes to handle deposits or full payments outside the official booking platform, it is a serious red flag in vacation rental guest screening. Off-platform transactions eliminate dispute resolution protections and make fraud recovery nearly impossible. Hosts receiving stolen credit card information may also be targeted this way. The tradeoff: some legitimate API-connected property managers do require secondary payment portals, so always verify directly with the platform before acting. 4. Vague or Evasive Answers About the Purpose of the Stay During vacation rental guest screening, guests who refuse to answer basic questions about why they are visiting, who they are traveling with, or what they plan to do during their stay are exhibiting a classic evasion pattern. Legitimate travelers typically share trip context willingly. Evasive responses often correlate with unauthorized parties, subletting, or commercial use of the property. The tradeoff: some introverted guests simply dislike small talk, so one unanswered question alone should not trigger a denial. 5. Last-Minute Bookings for Extended Stays A booking request made the same day or the day before for a stay of seven or more nights is a notable red flag in vacation rental guest screening. Genuine vacationers rarely plan extended trips with zero lead time, while individuals seeking temporary housing, fleeing a situation, or attempting fraud often do. This pattern becomes more suspicious when combined with a new profile or vague answers. The tradeoff: last-minute extended bookings occasionally come from legitimate corporate travelers or emergency relocations. 6. Use of Stolen or Mismatched Identity Information Scammers increasingly book vacation rentals using stolen credit card details or colluding with insiders to provide fraudulent identity verification. During vacation rental guest screening, mismatches between the name on the booking, the ID submitted, and the payment method are serious warning signs. Hosts using direct booking websites are especially vulnerable. The tradeoff: identity verification tools add friction that can deter legitimate guests, so the screening process must balance security with a smooth booking experience. 7. Negative or Retaliatory Reviews Left on Previous Stays A guest profile showing a pattern of low ratings given to previous hosts, or hosts who left cautionary reviews about rule violations, is a critical signal in vacation rental guest screening. Five-star review counts alone do not tell the full story, what a guest says about past hosts reveals their expectations and behavior. Hosts should read outgoing reviews carefully, not just incoming ones. The tradeoff: a single negative review may reflect a genuinely bad host experience rather than a problematic guest. Top Automated Guest Screening Software Tools and What Each Specializes In Not every guest screening tool was built to solve the same problem, and for multi-property operators, choosing by name recognition alone can mean paying for coverage that misses the exposures that actually keep you up at night. The tools compared below each emerged from a distinct gap in the market, from identity verification to damage protection to post-booking communication, so the comparison is less about ranking features and more about matching the right tool to the risk you are genuinely trying to close. Conduit.ai sits at the top of that list for a reason that goes beyond screening itself. Vacation Rental Guest Screening Software Compared - Top Tools for 2026 The "verification badge" that OTA platforms display to hosts is not a risk signal, it is a conversion signal engineered to reduce booking friction for the platform's revenue model. That distinction matters because multi-property operators who treat platform verification as a first-pass risk filter are unknowingly conflating identity confirmation with risk assessment, leaving their entire direct-booking channel and every edge-case OTA booking systematically unscreened. Not all guest screening software is built to solve the same problem. The tools that dominate this category each emerged from a different gap in the market, which means choosing by name recognition alone is one of the more expensive mistakes a multi-property operator can make. The comparison below is less about features and more about which exposure you are actually trying to close. 1. Conduit.ai - Best Overall AI-Powered Vacation Rental Guest Screening Conduit.ai earns the top slot not because it replaces identity checks or background databases, but because it solves the problem every other tool on this list leaves open: what happens immediately after a booking clears. Most operators assume the hard work ends at "Approved," but the communication layer that follows, welcome messages, rental agreement reminders, pre-arrival instructions, is where screened guests either become five-star reviews or support escalations. Conduit's AI-powered guest communication layer triggers personalized pre-arrival sequences the moment a booking clears, without a staff member touching the thread. It is most beneficial when managing 20 or more properties, where manual post-approval follow-up degrades under volume. 2. Truvi - Best for Comprehensive Identity Verification at Scale Truvi is purpose-built for operators who need fraud-signal detection before a guest ever reaches the property. Its automated checks span VPN and burner-phone detection, sex offender watchlists, and criminal background databases across 2,400-plus sources with a seven-year lookback, according to its product documentation. It automatically verifies contact details, scans for VPN and burner-phone use, checks sex offender watchlists, and delivers a clear Approved, Flagged, or Rejected verdict in the dashboard. Optional add-ons include criminal background checks across 2,400-plus databases with a seven-year lookback and up to $1 million in damage protection. The tradeoff: Truvi's strength is front-end fraud detection, so operators who need post-screening communication automation will still require a separate layer for guest coordination after the verdict lands. 3. Authenticate.com - Best for Criminal Background Check Depth Authenticate.com is the right pick when criminal record depth is the primary gap. Its background check infrastructure reaches county, federal, and international databases, a scope that goes materially beyond what any major OTA badge covers, as confirmed by Airbnb's own help documentation, which limits platform verification to name, photo, and document match. Deeper database searches take longer to return results, creating friction in high-velocity booking windows where guests expect near-instant confirmation, a genuine constraint for direct booking sites with fast checkout flows. 4. Superhog - Best for Damage Protection Bundled with Guest Screening Superhog combines biometric identity verification, matching a live selfie to a government-issued ID, with damage deposit management and a property damage guarantee typically ranging from $5,000 to $50,000 depending on the plan, according to its product documentation. Guests complete verification in under five minutes, and the platform integrates directly with PMS tools including Hostaway and Lodgify. Operators with high-value properties should confirm whether the guarantee replaces or supplements a traditional security deposit, because the coverage cap may not match replacement costs for premium furnishings. 5. Safely - Best for Instant Screening Decisions on Direct Booking Sites Safely is engineered for speed, delivering automated guest screening decisions in under 30 seconds, a critical advantage for hosts running direct booking websites where friction kills conversions. It screens for criminal history, fraud signals, and identity mismatches while issuing a guest guarantee to the host. The main limitation is that its screening model is proprietary and opaque, so hosts who want granular control over screening criteria or raw report data may find it insufficiently transparent. How the PMS-to-Screening Webhook Loop Actually Works Automated screening works through a webhook: the moment a booking is created in your PMS, a signal fires to your screening tool, which runs its checks and returns a risk score or status. The booking has to trigger the webhook. The webhook has to reach the screening tool without a timeout. The result has to route back to the right inbox, with the right alert, reaching someone with authority to act. Each handoff is a point where the process can quietly break without anyone noticing until a guest is already at the door. Instead of a flag routing to whichever VA happens to be logged in, every signal lands in a single monitored surface. The structural gap between "the tool flagged it" and "a human with authority saw it" narrows to seconds, not hours. The Overnight Booking Problem Most platforms give hosts a narrow window to cancel without penalty. When the flag and the cancellation window don't overlap with staffed hours, the process fails regardless of how well the screening criteria are configured. The tool did its job. The workflow didn't. Easy BnB's experience is instructive here: the vast majority of their communication volume was low-value messages that still required a human to read, triage, and respond before anything actionable could happen. That load meant overnight shifts were consumed by noise, leaving the high-stakes flags, the ones with a closing cancellation window, buried. An AI agent that handles repetitive, low-value guest messages continuously, before, during, and after a stay, frees the human review layer for the decisions that actually carry risk. Inconsistent Team Execution at 20-Plus Properties The failure mode that scales fastest is also the least visible: different staff members applying screening criteria differently under time pressure. One team member follows the full checklist. Another, handling a queue of eight bookings on a Friday afternoon, skips the manual review step for guests with a "Verified" badge. Neither decision gets logged. The dominant assumption is that better checklists fix inconsistency, when the actual problem is structural : no single enforced workflow means no consistent output, regardless of how experienced the team is. Workflows that trigger automatically after a booking is confirmed, rather than relying on a staff member to remember the next step, remove the discretion that produces variance. When a trigger event fires the same sequence every time, the checklist stops being a document someone consults and becomes a process that runs. For operators managing recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action, this is the structural fix that checklists cannot provide. It also directly addresses the portfolio scaling problem: you can grow the number of properties without growing the coordination headcount required to keep execution consistent across all of them. Integration Lag and Misconfigured Automations Webhook-based integrations between PMS platforms and third-party screening tools are not instantaneous. Processing delays, API timeouts, and misconfigured automation triggers can create windows where a booking is confirmed and access credentials are sent before the screening result returns. The short-term rental market has declined year-over-year, compressing the margin operators have to absorb the cost of a bad booking. In that environment, integration failures that were previously a nuisance become a direct threat to unit economics. Integrations that allow the AI agent to leverage existing content from tools like Notion, Google Drive, or Airbnb, without manual re-entry, reduce the configuration surface where mismatches and lag typically originate, keeping the loop tighter from the moment a booking is created. After Screening Passes - The Guest Communication Layer That Determines Your Review Score Screening a guest and serving a guest are two completely different operational problems. The first happens once, before check-in. The second happens continuously, from booking confirmation until the guest leaves a review. Most property managers invest heavily in the first and assume the second takes care of itself. It does not. The Hidden Cost Screening Never Eliminates - Communication Friction for Good Guests A vetted guest with five-star reviews and a verified ID can still leave a three-star rating. The reason is almost never who they are; it is what they experienced after approval: a check-in message that arrived 45 minutes late, a maintenance question unanswered until morning, a door code never confirmed. According to data tracked by Airbnb and Vrbo, response time is a direct ranking signal , and platforms algorithmically suppress listings where hosts reply slowly, regardless of how carefully those hosts screened their guests. The cost compounds: slower response times reduce search visibility, which reduces booking volume, which reduces the revenue that justified portfolio expansion. Screening and communication are not sequential phases. They are a single compounding system, and operators who treat them as separate trade the risk of one bad stay for the certainty of ongoing algorithmic suppression. Why Review Scores Degrade at Volume Even When Your Screening Is Airtight The pattern is consistent across growing portfolios: screening criteria stay tight, but review scores drift downward past 20 or 30 units. The root cause is response consistency, not guest quality. At five units, one person covers overnight messages. At 50, that same person cannot, and the 2am question from a perfectly screened guest goes unanswered until 7am. Hosts in larger operations frequently trace their worst reviews to communication gaps: a delayed response to a broken thermostat, a check-in instruction that arrived after the guest was already at the door. These are coordination failures no screening tool addresses. The 8-Step Screening Sequence Every Booking Must Clear, In Order A reliable booking approval process runs the same steps in the same order, every time: (1) confirm the inquiry communicates a clear purpose; (2) verify identity against a government-issued ID; (3) review guest history and prior host ratings; (4) ask targeted questions about group composition; (5) require explicit agreement to house rules before confirmation; (6) collect a security deposit or damage waiver; (7) run an automated risk score through your screening tool; and (8) route any flagged booking to a named decision-maker before the cancellation window closes. Consistency Is the Differentiator - Why Multi-Property Operators Fail at Step 7, Not Step 1 Operators managing 20-plus properties rarely fail at step 1. They fail at step 7, when booking volume spikes and the automated risk score never fires because an integration was misconfigured on a new channel, or because the one team member who knew how to read the flag was unavailable. The gap is not a knowledge problem. It is an infrastructure problem: who, or what, is watching every conversation across every platform at every hour. This is precisely where an AI-first operations layer changes the equation. Workflows handle the recurring, predictable touchpoints, post-booking confirmation messages, pre-check-in rule acknowledgment requests, security deposit reminders, triggered automatically when a booking is confirmed or a specific keyword is detected, without manual staff action. The goal is a systemized, scalable business that does not depend entirely on owner involvement. That does not mean removing human decision-makers from step 8. It means ensuring steps 1 through 7 never quietly skip themselves because your volume exceeded your bandwidth. What most teams report at scale is this: that execution consistency, not the sophistication of the criteria, is what defines top-performing operators at scale. Next steps If your screening criteria are solid but your outcomes are still uneven across properties and time zones, the path forward starts with treating this as a structural problem, not a discipline problem. Inconsistent execution at scale is not fixed by a tighter checklist. It is fixed by a communication and verification layer that runs identically at 2pm and 2am, across every unit in the portfolio. title: Introducing Frontier AI Model Platforms — Because An AI Model Is Not A Business Model
